blocks.text: Growth and Decay in Finance (Predicting Long-Term Stock Prices)

When something increases in quantity or size over time, it is called growth. For example, money in a bank account earning interest (it grows larger), a population of rabbits is increasing over months.
When something decreases in quantity or size over time, it is called decay. For example, a radioactive substance is losing its strength over years, a cup of hot coffee is cooling down over time.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Exponential growth: \(P(t) = P_{0}e^{rt}\), with \(r > 0\). Here \(P_{0}\) is the starting value (at \(t = 0\), \(e^{0} = 1\)), \(r\) is the rate as a decimal (5% = 0.05) and \(e \approx 2.71828\). The value grows faster and faster because each year's growth is a percentage of a bigger amount.
To find a time that sits in the exponent, take the natural logarithm \(\ln\), which undoes \(e\): if \(e^{k} = a\) then \(k = \ln a\).
Decay is the opposite: the quantity goes down over time, as in Example 13.

blocks.title: Example 12
blocks.problem:
The value of a stock follows the exponential growth model \(P(t) = P_{0}e^{rt}\), where \(P_{0}\) is the initial stock price, \(r\) is the growth rate per year and \(t\) is the time in years. Suppose a stock is currently valued at Rs. 5,000, and it is expected to grow at a rate of 5% per year.
(i) Find the value of the stock after 10 years.
(ii) After how many years will the stock double in value?
steps:
Given: \(P(t) = P_{0}e^{rt}\) with \(P_{0} = 5{,}000\), \(r = 0.05\) (5% growth rate).
To find: (i) \(P(10)\); (ii) the time \(t\) at which \(P(t) = 2P_{0}\).
Method: (i) substitute the values into the formula; (ii) set \(P(t) = 2P_{0}\) and solve for \(t\) by taking the natural logarithm, because \(t\) is in the exponent.

Step 1: (i) Substitute \(t = 10\)
The formula for the exponential growth is \(P(t) = P_{0}e^{rt}\). Given \(P_{0} = 5{,}000\), \(r = 0.05\) and \(t = 10\) years.
The book prints: \(P(10) = 5.000\, e^{0.05 \times 10}\) \(= 5{,}000\, e^{0.5}\).
Working it out:
\[P(10) = 5{,}000\, e^{0.05 \times 10}\]
\[= 5{,}000\, e^{0.5}\]
Why: a rate of 5% is \(r = \frac{5}{100} = 0.05\); and \(0.05 \times 10 = 0.5\).

Step 2: (i) Evaluate
Using \(e^{0.5} \approx 1.6487\):
\[P(10) = 5{,}000 \times 1.6487\]
\[\approx 8244\]
Why: \(e \approx 2.71828\) is the base of natural growth; a calculator gives \(e^{0.5} \approx 1.6487\). (Exactly, \(5{,}000 \times 1.648721\ldots = 8243.6\), which rounds to Rs. 8244.)

Step 3: (ii) Write the doubling condition
We want to find \(t\) when the stock doubles, i.e., when \(P(t) = 2P_{0}\). Using the equation:
\[2P_{0} = P_{0}e^{rt}\]
Dividing both sides by \(P_{0}\), we have
\[2 = e^{rt}\]
Why: "double in value" means twice the starting price. \(P_{0}\) cancels, so the doubling time does not depend on the starting price.

Step 4: (ii) Take the natural logarithm
\[\ln 2 = rt\]
Why: \(\ln\) undoes \(e\): \(\ln(e^{rt}) = rt\). This brings \(t\) down from the exponent.

Step 5: (ii) Solve for \(t\)
The book prints: \(t = \ln 2 / r = 0.69310.05 = 13.86\)
Working it out:
\[t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{r} = \dfrac{0.6931}{0.05}\]
\[t \approx 13.86\]
Why: \(\ln 2 \approx 0.6931\); dividing by \(0.05\) is the same as multiplying by 20.

Check:
(i) \(\ln(8244 / 5000) = \ln 1.6488 \approx 0.5 = 0.05 \times 10\).
(ii) \(e^{0.05 \times 13.86} = e^{0.693} \approx 2.00\), so after 13.86 years the value is twice the start.
blocks.answer:
(i) After 10 years the stock is worth approximately Rs. 8244.
(ii) The stock will double in value in approximately 13.86 years.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
Two misprints in the solution of Example 12:
(i) the book prints \(P(10) = 5.000\, e^{0.05 \times 10}\) with a decimal point; it should be \(5{,}000\, e^{0.05 \times 10}\) (five thousand), as the next expression shows.
(ii) the book prints \(t = \ln 2 / r = 0.69310.05 = 13.86\) with the division sign missing; it should be \(t = \ln 2 / r = 0.6931 / 0.05 = 13.86\).

blocks.title: Example 13
blocks.problem:
The concentration of a pollutant in a lake, in parts per million (ppm), decays over time according to the function
\[C(t) = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{t + 1}}\]
where \(t\) is the time in days since the pollutant was introduced.
(i) What is the concentration of the pollutant after 4 days?
(ii) After how many days will the concentration drop below 10 ppm?
steps:
Given: \(C(t) = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{t + 1}}\), \(t\) in days.
To find: (i) \(C(4)\); (ii) the time after which \(C(t) < 10\).
Method: (i) substitute \(t = 4\); (ii) find when \(C(t) = 10\) (the book sets \(C(t) = 10\)), then use the fact that \(C\) decreases as \(t\) grows.

Step 1: (i) Concentration after 4 days
The pollutant concentration function is \(C(t) = \frac{100}{\sqrt{t + 1}}\), where \(t\) is the time in days.
\[C(4) = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{4 + 1}} = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{5}}\]
\[\approx 44.72 \text{ ppm}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.2361\) and \(100 / 2.2361 \approx 44.72\).

Step 2: (ii) Set \(C(t) = 10\)
\[10 = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{t + 1}}\]
\[\Rightarrow \sqrt{t + 1} = 10\]
Why: multiply both sides by \(\sqrt{t + 1}\) and divide by 10: \(\sqrt{t + 1} = 100 / 10\).

Step 3: (ii) Square and solve
\[t + 1 = 100\]
\[\Rightarrow t = 99\]
Why: squaring removes the square root; both sides are positive, so no extra solution appears.

Step 4: (ii) Interpret
At \(t = 99\) the concentration is exactly 10 ppm. As \(t\) increases, \(\sqrt{t + 1}\) increases, so \(C(t)\) decreases; therefore after 99 days the concentration is below 10 ppm.
Why: the question asks "below 10", so we need the direction in which \(C\) changes, not only the moment it equals 10.

Check:
\[C(99) = \dfrac{100}{\sqrt{100}} = 10\]
\[C(120) = \dfrac{100}{11} \approx 9.09 < 10\]
Also \(C(4) = 44.72\) is between \(C(0) = 100\) and \(C(99) = 10\), as expected for a decreasing function.
blocks.answer:
(i) After 4 days the concentration is about 44.72 ppm.
(ii) After 99 days the concentration will drop below 10 ppm (it is exactly 10 ppm at \(t = 99\)).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Growth: the quantity increases with time; decay: it decreases.
2. Exponential growth \(P(t) = P_{0}e^{rt}\): write the rate as a decimal; \(P(0) = P_{0}\).
3. Doubling time: \(t = \frac{\ln 2}{r} \approx \frac{0.6931}{r}\), whatever the starting value.
4. To solve for a variable in the exponent, take \(\ln\) of both sides.
5. For "drop below" questions, solve the equality, then use whether the function is increasing or decreasing.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Using \(r = 5\) instead of \(r = 0.05\).
2. Writing \(\ln(e^{rt}) = e^{rt}\) or forgetting to divide by \(r\).
3. In Example 13, writing \(C(4) = 100/\sqrt{4} + 1\): the \(+1\) is inside the square root, \(\sqrt{4 + 1} = \sqrt{5}\).
4. Rounding too early: keep four decimal places of \(e^{0.5}\) and \(\ln 2\) until the last step.
